newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-EU official criticises Bonn's tough EMU line.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU official criticises Bonn's tough EMU line.

text.p: A German European Commissioner has sharply criticised Bonn's tough stand on meeting entry goals for currency union and said Germany should have an escape clause to squeeze into EMU.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel last week revived tough rhetoric by demanding that governments wanting to join economic and monetary union should keep their budget deficits to 3.0 percent of gross doemstic product (GDP).
But in an interview published on Friday, Commissioner Monika Wulf Mathies said the Maastricht Treaty, which set targets for EMU entry, was less specific.
If countries achieved slightly higher numbers, this should not derail the project, she said.
Lashing out a what she called Bonn's "percent acrobatics", Wulf Mathies told the Berliner Morgenpost newspaper that the prevailing viewpoint "no longer had anything in common with economic sense".
Even with a budget deficit of 3.2 percent, the Treaty did not foresee postponing EMU's scheduled launch date of January 1, 1999, Wulf Mathies said.
"The number 3.0 percent is not written in the Maastricht Treaty. Currency union is not some numbers lottery but rather a conscious political decision," she said.
Germany has been demanding strict compliance with the targets to protect the credibility of the new euro currency.

But quibbling over exactly what the Treaty's "three" percent reference value means has become a hot topic as Germany struggles to meet its 1997 deficit goal of 2.9 percent due to high unemployment and fragile growth.
Bonn is holding firm to forecasts that last year's 3.8 percent deficit can be slashed to 2.9 percent this year but most independent economists see a rate above three percent.
Wulf Mathies said a realistic chance remained that Germany could fulfil this goal without making some sort of accounting detour.

But the commissioner, who was formerly head of Germany's public sector service union OeTV, also urged that Bonn be granted special treatment, taking into consideration the high cost of German unification.

European Union finance ministers have already assured Waigel that unification of the former west and communist east Germanies had to be taken into account when assessing Germany's debt levels for monetary union.
Unification costs were responsible for more than half of a surge in total debt to 2.135 trillion marks ($1.2 trillion) at the end of 1996 from 929 billion in 1989, the Bundesbank said recently.

But Bonn has shied away from demanding special attention on the deficit criterion to avoid playing into the hands of some southern nations -- notably Italy -- which might try to use the same tactic to gain EMU entry, economists have said.

If Germany should fail to meet the stability criteria the Treaty would justify an exemption due to exceptional circumstances, Wulf Mathies said. Without the costs of unification, Germany's fiscal data would "look quite different", she added.
She also believed enough EU member nations would fulfil the convergence criteria, saying this would not necessarily mean all criteria would be fulfiled to the decimal point.

Economists feel even Bonn's tough stance might soften slightly this autumn if Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the driving force behind European integration, signals he is willing to tolerate a slight overshooting.
"The government is not going to let EMU collapse," Stefan Schneider, economist at Banque Paribas in Frankfurt said.

On the other hand, the government also left no doubts about its tolerance level. Finance Ministry official Klaus Regling on Tuesday said: "I can't expect Germany would allow a nation to participate in EMU with a deficit of 3.5 percent."
